opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one of the things we thought about quite a bit. The core of Rainbow Teaming is an open-ended search: we keep an archive of adversarial prompts organized along dimensions like risk category and attack style, and we're constantly mutating prompts to fill that grid with more diverse and more effective attacks. To decide whether a new prompt should replace the one currently sitting in a cell, you need some notion of which one is "better," and that's where a judge comes in.

One design choice that mattered a lot was making the judgment comparative rather than absolute. Instead of asking a model to give a response a harmfulness score from one to ten, which tends to be noisy and poorly calibrated, we show the judge two responses from the target model and ask which one is more unsafe. Language models are much more reliable at relative comparisons than absolute scoring. It's similar to why pairwise preferences work well in RLHF.

Your question gets at a real tension, though. Whenever you optimize against a model-based evaluator, you risk the search finding the judge's blind spots rather than genuine vulnerabilities in the target. That's basically Goodhart's law. If the same model or model family is generating, attacking, and judging, you might worry it'll systematically miss failure modes it shares with itself, or that the search will drift toward prompts that look scary to the judge but aren't actually harmful.

So we tried to mitigate that in a few ways. We didn't rely only on the judge used during search. We evaluated the final archives with independent classifiers like Llama Guard and also did human evaluation, to check that the attack success rates we were seeing were real and not artifacts of the judge. The pairwise setup also helps, because it only needs to be locally consistent. It just has to tell you whether you're making progress in a given cell.

More broadly, I think this is part of a bigger shift. As models become more capable, using models to evaluate and stress-test other models, or even themselves, becomes unavoidable, because humans can't label at that scale or with that diversity. But you have to treat the judge as a fallible component in the loop. You need to ground it periodically with independent signals. And the nice thing is that the outputs of Rainbow Teaming become training data. When we fine-tuned on the discovered attacks, the models became substantially more robust without losing general capability. That closes the loop: the system finds its own weaknesses and helps fix them. To me that's the really exciting open-endedness angle. It's a process that keeps generating new challenges rather than a static benchmark that eventually saturates.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the more subtle parts of the whole setup, and it's something we spent a lot of time thinking about. Rainbow Teaming is essentially a quality-diversity approach to adversarial prompt generation. We're using a MAP-Elites style archive where the dimensions are things like the risk category, the attack style, and so on. And in order to fill that archive, you need some way of scoring candidate prompts, both in terms of whether they actually elicit an unsafe response from the target, and in terms of where they sit in that feature space.

The natural thing to do is to use a language model as the judge, because asking humans to label tens of thousands of prompts and responses is just not feasible at the scale we need for this kind of open-ended search. But the moment you do that, you have to be quite careful, because you're essentially optimizing against a learned proxy. And anything that is optimized against hard enough will eventually be gamed. So if the judge has blind spots, the search process will find those blind spots and exploit them, and you'll end up with "adversarial prompts" that are really just adversarial to the judge rather than genuinely harmful.

A few things we did to mitigate this. One is that we don't ask the judge for an absolute score. We frame it as a pairwise comparison, so the judge is looking at two responses to two candidate prompts and saying which one is more unsafe. That turned out to be a lot more reliable than asking the model to output a number from one to ten, because these models are quite poorly calibrated on absolute scales but reasonably good at relative judgments. Another thing is that we were mindful about which model does the judging versus which model is being attacked. If it's the same model, you can get a kind of self-consistency bias, where the model is reluctant to call its own outputs unsafe. So decoupling those roles helps.

And then the last piece is that we actually validated against human annotators. We took a sample of the archive and had people check whether the judge's assessments held up, and the agreement was high enough that we were comfortable with the approach. But I'd be the first to say it's not a solved problem. The judge is part of the attack surface, in a sense, and as these systems get more capable I think we'll need to think about the robustness of the evaluator just as seriously as the robustness of the target. There's a lot of interesting work to do there, including potentially using the same kind of open-ended search to red-team the judge itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the important distinction is between using the model as a generator and using it as a judge. Generating a jailbreak means finding a prompt that causes a target model to produce an unsafe response. Judging means looking at that response and deciding whether the attack actually succeeded. A model can have quite different capabilities on those two tasks, so using a language model as a judge can be useful even when it’s also involved in generating attacks.

But I wouldn’t treat that judgment as ground truth. The judge can make mistakes, and when you’re repeatedly selecting attacks based on its feedback, you risk finding attacks that exploit the judge’s weaknesses rather than the target model’s safety weaknesses. So I’d view it as a scalable feedback signal for the search, with independent checks to establish whether the resulting jailbreaks really work. In Rainbow Teaming, you also care about finding a diverse collection of successful attacks, rather than optimizing a single example against a single judge.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes generation from judging and says they require different capabilities, but does not state that verifying candidates is easier than generating them.

r002.rationale: It does not describe retaining a generated jailbreak when a judge rates it as more effective than a previously generated one.

r003.rationale: It mentions independent checks, but does not specify held-out empirical evaluation or compare its results with the system’s own effectiveness assessments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be careful about what you mean by judging. The model proposing a jailbreak and the model judging whether that jailbreak succeeded are doing different jobs. You can ask a judge to look at the target model’s response and assess whether it actually fulfilled the harmful request, rather than simply checking whether it refused.

But that judge is still an imperfect signal. It can make mistakes, and if you optimize against it, you can discover ways of exploiting the judge rather than finding genuine vulnerabilities in the target. So I’d view it as a way to scale the search, rather than as definitive evidence that an attack worked. You still want independent validation, including human inspection, to establish how reliable those judgments are.
